"Pith" has two main families of meaning — one literal (physical), one figurative — plus an older, less common sense worth knowing. Understanding all three will give you the complete picture.
1. The Physical Meaning: The Core of a Plant

Pith is the soft, spongy, white tissue found at the center of plant stems. If you snap a sunflower stalk in half or slice through a branch of elder, you'll see firm outer walls and a light, crumbly white core inside — that's pith. Think of it as nature's foam padding built into the inside of a stem.

The same word also refers to the white, spongy layer inside citrus fruits — the bitter, stringy material that sits between the bright outer peel and the juicy fruit segments of an orange, lemon, or grapefruit. Many cooks and recipes tell you to remove it because it tastes bitter.

So: pith is always the soft, central, or inner substance of something in nature.

A side note worth knowing: pith helmets (the rounded, lightweight colonial-era safari helmets) were named after this word — they were originally made from the dried, harvested pith of certain tropical plants, which made them extremely light and good at blocking heat.
2. The Figurative Meaning: The Essential Core of an Idea

This is where "pith" really shines, and it's the sense you'll encounter most often in books, essays, and formal writing.

When used figuratively, pith means the most important, essential, central part of something — especially of a speech, an argument, a piece of writing, or a complex topic. The logic is the same: just as pith is the core substance inside a stem, the "pith" of an idea is the core substance inside it — the thing everything else wraps around.

Think of it as the answer to the question: "If I stripped away all the padding and extra words, what's the real heart of this?" That heart is the pith.

Examples:

  • "The pith of her argument was simple: people fear change more than they fear failure."

Here, "pith" = the essential point she was making, once all the supporting details are removed.

  • "He finally got to the pith of the matter after an hour of talking."

= He finally reached the real, core issue.

  • "That single paragraph contains the pith of the entire 300-page book."

= The essential meaning of the whole book is concentrated there.

You can think of it as a fancier, more precise word for essence, core, or heart — but with a slightly stronger suggestion that everything non-essential has been stripped away.
3. The Older Meaning: Vigor, Substance, or Force

In older writing (and occasionally still today), "pith" was used to mean strength, substance, or weight — the quality that makes a person, a speech, or a piece of work feel solid and powerful rather than weak and hollow.

  • "A man of great pith" — a person of strong character and force.
  • "Writing of no pith" — weak, hollow, insubstantial writing.
  • "His words carried pith." — His words had real weight and impact.

You're most likely to see this sense in Shakespeare, the King James Bible, or 19th-century prose. It's rare in modern everyday speech, but it does pop up in literary writing.

All three senses share the same underlying idea: dense, essential substance at the core. Pith in a plant is the substance at the core of the stem. Pith of an argument is the substance at the core of the idea. Pith as vigor is the core substance of a person's character or a work's quality. The word always points inward, toward what's most real and central.
The Word "Pithy" — Its Most Common Descendant

From "pith" comes the adjective pithy, which you'll encounter very often and which is worth knowing here. Something described as pithy is brief but dense with meaning — short, sharp, and straight to the point, with no wasted words. A pithy remark or a pithy saying packs a lot of substance into very few words.

  • "'Actions speak louder than words' is a pithy observation."
  • "She gave a pithy two-sentence summary of a two-hour meeting."

The logic: good plant pith is dense and full. Pithy speech or writing is similarly dense — small in volume, but full of substance.

  • Figurative (most important): The essential, central meaning or point of an idea, speech, or argument.

  • Related word: Pithy = brief but full of meaning.
